title: Two Ways to Make It Less Complicated
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. invokes Parkinson's Law, the observation that work expands to fill the time available, and applies it to the work of schools. He lists corollaries for initiatives, units, grading, and the teaching job itself, then argues the only remedy is constraint rather than a blank check of time. He offers two practical questions to force simplification: what would this look like if I only had one hour, and what would I do if I had to be done by a certain date? The second is applied concretely to fixed unit end dates set before the school year starts, which he says protect the end of the course from disruptions and make complicated decisions into non-decisions. The piece closes by asking readers for their own anti-complexity practices.
points: Parkinson's Law has direct school corollaries: initiatives, units, grading, and workload all swell to fill whatever time or committee size they are given.
Constraint is the proposed fix, whether that means a daily thirty-minute email window or an artificially short deadline for a task.
Asking what a task would look like in one hour forces simplifications that open-ended time never produces, whether for reading a book or building a unit.
Fixing unit start and end dates in advance means the course stays balanced, and the cost of disruptions is absorbed along the way rather than at the end of the year.
Firm end dates reduce stress because they turn recurring judgment calls into settled non-decisions.
quotes: The only way to solve for Parkinson’s Law is constraint. Instead of giving yourself or your committee a blank check, you have to add simple rules or constraints. For example, I get to check my email once per day for 30 minutes.

The law describes “the commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.” While you can almost see the wry smile on his face from the tone of Parkinson’s article, more important words for educators were rarely written in the 1950s or since.

Try creating that next unit in one hour. You’ll skip Googling it, getting lost on blogs, or buying a set of worksheets on Teachers Pay Teachers. Instead, you’ll start with the end and ask yourself what the best paths are to get there.

Instead of letting time, disruptions, and snow days rule my courses, I set start and end dates, and I stick to them. Sometimes, I’m forced to teach part of a unit much more quickly than I’d like. But I never end up rushed at the end of the year, and my students end up getting a balanced version of the course much more consistently than they did before I started this practice.

I figure that for every child who might like that extra day of a unit, there is another that would rather move on. Unit end dates, decided before the school year even begins, help make would-be complex decisions into non-decisions.

It is remarkably simpler for all involved in my courses to know that, no matter what, we’ll be finishing the unit next Friday. I’d rather eat the costs of disruptions now than save them up for the end of the school year.
